For a $10,000 loan at 6% nominal interest over 36 months with $300 upfront fees, the unrounded monthly payment is about $304.21937452. Total payments round to $10,951.90 and proceeds are $9,700. Compare both readings with the AHA adult blood pressure categories and use the higher category reached. A reading of 135/85 mmHg is in Stage 1. This reference is not designed for children, pregnancy or conditions that require different clinical criteria.

Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic. Adult reference categories follow the American Heart Association chart. Use the higher category reached by either reading; normal and elevated categories require both stated conditions. Very high readings do not alone establish a hypertensive emergency.

135/85: systolic 135 falls in 130–139 (Stage 1) and diastolic 85 falls in 80–89 (Stage 1), so the category is Stage 1 hypertension. Pulse pressure = 135 − 85 = 50 mmHg. A single reading does not diagnose hypertension — diagnosis rests on repeated readings over time, interpreted by a clinician.

This is an adult category reference, not diagnosis or treatment advice. It does not assess children, pregnancy, low blood pressure or the cause of symptoms. Measurement technique and repeated readings matter; a clinician interprets the result with your history.
What do the two numbers mean?
Systolic is the pressure when the heart contracts; diastolic is the pressure between beats. Both matter — the category uses whichever falls in the higher band.
Does one high reading mean I have hypertension?
No. Diagnosis requires repeated elevated readings over time, usually including readings taken outside the clinic. A single high reading is a reason to recheck, not a diagnosis.
Why is my clinic reading higher than at home?
White-coat effect: stress in a clinical setting raises readings for many people. Home readings taken with correct technique are often lower and are part of the diagnostic picture.
How should I measure blood pressure accurately?

Seated, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart height, correct cuff size, no caffeine or exercise in the prior 30 minutes, and a few minutes of rest first. Two readings a minute apart, averaged, beat one rushed reading.
The gap between systolic and diastolic — 50 mmHg in the example. A wide gap can reflect stiff arteries, but it is interpreted alongside the absolute numbers, not alone.
When should I seek urgent care?

A very high reading with chest pain, trouble breathing, weakness, vision changes or difficulty speaking needs emergency help immediately. Without these symptoms, wait at least one minute and measure again. If it remains over 180 systolic or 120 diastolic, contact a healthcare professional promptly.

Adult categories: underweight below 18.5; healthy weight from 18.5 to less than 25; overweight from 25 to less than 30; obesity from 30. The bar uses a scale of 40.

BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²). BMI Prime = BMI ÷ 25. Ponderal Index = weight (kg) ÷ height³ (m³). The reference weight interval starts at 18.5 × height² and ends just below 25 × height². Displayed thresholds are rounded; the upper threshold is excluded.

At 175 cm and 72.6 kg: BMI = 72.6 ÷ 1.75² ≈ 23.7, BMI Prime ≈ 0.95, and Ponderal Index ≈ 13.5 kg/m³. The reference weight thresholds are 18.5 × 1.75² = 56.65625 kg and 25 × 1.75² = 76.5625 kg, with the upper threshold excluded. Rounded for display: 56.7–<76.6 kg. Molar mass in g/mol = Σ (number of atoms of each element × its tabulated atomic weight). For Ca(OH)2, the subscript 2 multiplies both O and H: Ca + 2 × O + 2 × H. The fixed table uses rounded values such as H 1.008, C 12.011, N 14.007 and O 15.999.

Using this table, H2O has molar mass 2 × 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol. Its calculated mass fractions are 2.016 ÷ 18.015 ≈ 11.19% hydrogen and 15.999 ÷ 18.015 ≈ 88.81% oxygen. Other table-based checks are CO2 = 12.011 + 2 × 15.999 = 44.009 g/mol and NaCl = 22.990 + 35.45 = 58.440 g/mol.

What is a mole in chemistry?
One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified elementary entities. Molar mass expresses the mass of one mole in g/mol; the displayed values use this calculator’s rounded atomic-weight table.

Hydrogen and oxygen use averaged atomic weights of 1.008 and 15.999 in this table. Therefore 2 × 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol. This is an approximate conventional value; an isotope-enriched sample can differ.

Fixed costs $50,000, price $200, variable cost $120: contribution margin is $200 − $120 = $80 per unit, so break-even units = $50,000 ÷ $80 = 625 units, and break-even revenue = 625 × $200 = $125,000.

Principal $10,000, $500 a month, 6% a year for 10 years (120 months): the principal grows to $18,193.97, the $60,000 of contributions grows to $81,939.67, for a future value of $100,133.64. Interest earned is $30,133.64 on $70,000 put in.

Daily cost is 4.80. The rate here is only the example default — your bill's actual rate is what matters.

Distance 500 km, economy 7.5 L/100 km, price 8 per litre, tolls and parking 100: fuel used = 500 ÷ 100 × 7.5 = 37.5 L, fuel cost = 37.50 × 8 = 300.00, trip cost = 300.00 + 100 = 400.00, or 0.80 per km. The fuel price here is only the example default — enter the price you actually expect to pay.

Grades 3.7 (3 credits), 3.3 (3 credits), 4.0 (4 credits) and 3.0 (2 credits): points are 11.1 + 9.9 + 16.0 + 6.0 = 43.0, over 12 credits, so GPA = 43.0 ÷ 12 = 3.5833. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result, then replace the values with your own.

Gross pay $6,000 per month, effective tax rate 15%, social contributions $500, other deductions $0: estimated tax = $6,000 × 0.15 = $900, net pay = $6,000 − $900 − $500 − $0 = $4,600 per month, or $55,200 per year.
Solve for current with V = 12 V and R = 4 Ω: I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 4 = 3.00 A. Power = V × I = 12 × 3 = 36.00 W. Check through the other form: P = V² ÷ R = 144 ÷ 4 = 36.00 W — consistent.

Area 120 m², 2 coats, coverage 10 m²/L: paint per coat = 120 ÷ 10 = 12 L, so 2 coats need 24 L. At a 10% waste allowance, waste = 24 × 0.10 = 2.4 L, giving 26.4 L required. These are the example defaults above; replace them with your own area and the coverage printed on your paint.

Price $199, cost $110, sales 1,000 units, increase 8%, volume decline 5%: new price = $199 × 1.08 = $214.92, new volume = 1,000 × 0.95 = 950 units, new profit = ($214.92 − $110) × 950 = $99,674, current profit = ($199 − $110) × 1,000 = $89,000, so profit rises by $10,674.

Acceleration
Velocity change:
Worked example

From rest (0 m/s) to 30 m/s in 5 seconds: a = (30 − 0) ÷ 5 = 6.00 m/s². The velocity change is 30 m/s, and the distance covered is ((0 + 30) ÷ 2) × 5 = 15 × 5 = 75 m. For scale, 6 m/s² is a brisk car launch — roughly 0 to 100 km/h in about 4.6 seconds at that rate (100 km/h is 27.78 m/s, and 27.78 ÷ 6 = 4.63 s).
FAQ
What is the difference between velocity and acceleration?

Velocity is how fast something moves; acceleration is how fast that velocity changes. A car cruising at a steady 30 m/s has high velocity and zero acceleration; the same car speeding up from 0 to 30 m/s has positive acceleration throughout.
What does a negative acceleration mean?
Why is the unit m/s²?
Because acceleration is velocity change per unit time: (m/s) ÷ s = m/s². It reads as "metres per second, per second" — each second, velocity grows by that many m/s.
How does this relate to force?
Newton's second law: force = mass × acceleration. A 1,000 kg car accelerating at 6 m/s² needs 6,000 N of net force. This page does not ask for mass, so it cannot report force.
Can I use km/h instead of m/s?
Only if you convert first: divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s, and convert time to seconds. Mixing km/h with seconds gives a number that is not m/s². The velocity calculator's conversions can help.
Is 9.8 m/s² special?
Yes — it is g, Earth's surface gravity. An object in free fall (ignoring air resistance) accelerates downward at about 9.81 m/s². Enter v₀ = 0, v₁ = 9.81, t = 1 to see it.

Age = reference date − date of birth, evaluated as a calendar difference: completed years first, then completed months, then remaining days. Days lived is the plain day count between the two dates. Days until the next birthday is the day count from the reference date to the next occurrence of the birth month and day.

Born 10 May 1990, at the reference date 28 October 2026: 36 completed years (to 10 May 2026), plus 5 completed months (to 10 October 2026), plus 18 days = 36 years, 5 months, 18 days. Days lived = 13,320 days. The next birthday is 10 May 2027, which is 194 days after 28 October 2026. Set the reference date to 2026-10-28 to reproduce this result.

All dates are local calendar dates; times of day and time zones are ignored, so a birthday later today still counts as reached on its date. Leap years are handled by the calendar itself: a person born on 29 February ages by completed calendar years, and in a non-leap year this page treats 28 February as the birthday for the next-birthday count (stated here so the convention is explicit, not assumed). If the date of birth is after the reference date, no age is shown.
Is the age in years, months and days exact?
Yes, as a calendar age: completed years, then completed months, then days. It is not total days divided by 365, which would drift across leap years.
How are leap years handled?
By the real calendar. The day count between two dates automatically includes 29 February in leap years, and the year/month breakdown follows calendar months of different lengths.
What about a 29 February birthday?
Age still advances by completed calendar years. For the next-birthday countdown in a non-leap year, this page uses 28 February and says so in the scope section.
Does time of day matter?
No. Only calendar dates are compared, so time zones and birth times do not change the result.
What if the birth date is in the future?
No result is shown; the page asks for a birth date on or before the reference date.

Energy (kWh) = calls × Wh per call × PUE ÷ 1,000. Emissions (kg CO₂e) = energy × grid grams per kWh ÷ 1,000. Per-call emissions (g CO₂e) = Wh per call × PUE × grid grams per kWh ÷ 1,000.

Calls 100,000, energy 0.5 Wh per call, PUE 1.2, grid 450 gCO₂e/kWh. Energy = 100,000 × 0.5 × 1.2 ÷ 1,000 = 60 kWh. Emissions = 60 × 450 ÷ 1,000 = 27 kg CO₂e. These inputs are examples only — replace the energy-per-call and grid figures with your own before relying on the result.

This is a scenario model, not a carbon accounting result. It covers only the inference energy you describe: training, model development, hardware manufacturing, networking, cooling beyond PUE, and embodied emissions are excluded. Energy per call varies by model, hardware, batching, and prompt length, and grid intensity varies by place and time — both are user inputs here precisely because no single published value fits every case. No live emissions data or certified accounting is provided.
How is this calculated?
Energy is calls times Wh per call times PUE, divided by 1,000 to get kWh; emissions are energy times grid grams per kWh, divided by 1,000 to get kilograms of CO₂e.
Why are the carbon factor and energy per call editable?
Because they are assumptions, not constants. A different model, GPU, or region gives different values, so the page treats them as inputs you must supply and labels the defaults as examples only.
What does PUE mean here?

Power usage effectiveness: total facility energy divided by IT energy. A PUE of 1.2 means 20% overhead for cooling and other facility loads on top of inference energy; 1.0 means no overhead is counted.
Does this include training the model?
No. It covers only the inference calls in your scenario. Training, fine-tuning, and hardware manufacturing are separate and much larger in some cases, and are not modeled here.
Why is the result linear in call count?

Each row in the volume table reuses the same per-call figure, so doubling calls doubles the estimate. Real systems may batch or cache, which would break that linearity — another reason to replace the example per-call figure with measured data.
Can I use this for an official emissions report?

No. It is a planning estimate from your own assumptions. Formal reporting needs measured energy data, a documented grid factor for the right region and period, and the reporting framework your organisation follows.

Is annualized return the same as average yearly return?
No. A simple average of yearly returns ignores compounding. The annualized (compound) rate is the single steady rate that reproduces the total growth over the period.
What if the final value is lower than the initial value?
The result is negative, which is correct: a negative annualized rate means the value shrank at that steady yearly pace.
Can I use it for periods shorter than a year?
Does it include dividends or fees?
Only if they are already reflected in the final value you enter. Dividends reinvested raise the final value; fees paid out lower it.
Why is it lower than the total return divided by years?
Because compounding does part of the work: 50% over 4 years is 10.67% compounded, not 12.50% a year, since each year's growth also earns growth in later years.
Why is APR higher than the interest rate?

Because APR spreads the fees across the loan as well as the interest. In the example, $300 of fees on a $10,000 loan lifts the cost from 6% to 8.06%. A loan with a lower rate but heavy fees can easily cost more than a higher-rate loan with no fees.
What is the difference between nominal and effective APR?
Nominal APR is 12 times the monthly rate (8.06% here). Effective APR compounds that monthly rate over a year ((1 + r)
− 1 = 8.36%). Lenders usually quote the nominal figure; the effective figure is what compounding actually costs.
Do I compare APRs or monthly payments?

Compare APRs for loans of the same term and structure — it is the only figure that includes fees. Monthly payments alone hide fees, and a longer term can look cheaper per month while costing far more overall.
What if the loan has no fees?

Then the amount received equals the loan amount, the solving rate equals the nominal monthly rate, and nominal APR equals the nominal rate. The effective APR is still slightly higher because interest compounds monthly.
Does a shorter term raise or lower APR?
With the same fees, a shorter term raises APR: the same $300 is spread over fewer payments, so each payment carries more fee cost. That is why small short loans often show startling APRs.
Is this the same APR my lender quotes?

It should be close if the inputs match and the lender counts the same charges. If it differs, check which fees the lender included or excluded, and whether the rate is fixed — a variable rate makes any single APR figure an estimate.

APR (nominal)
Effective APR:
Monthly payment:
Total paid:
First the monthly payment at the nominal rate: PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)

), where P is the loan amount, i is the monthly nominal rate, and n is the number of payments. APR is then the monthly rate r that makes the present value of those payments equal the amount actually received (P − fees): (P − fees) = PMT × (1 − (1 + r)
) ÷ r. The nominal APR is 12 × r; the effective APR is (1 + r)
− 1. The page solves for r by bisection, not by an approximation formula.
$10,000 at a 6% nominal rate over 36 months with $300 of upfront fees: the monthly payment is 10,000 × 0.005 ÷ (1 − 1.005

) = $304.22, and $304.22 × 36 = $10,951.90 is repaid in total. The borrower actually receives 10,000 − 300 = $9,700, and the monthly rate that discounts 36 payments of $304.22 back to $9,700 is 0.6714%, so the nominal APR is 12 × 0.6714% = 8.06% (8.36% effective). The $300 fee lifts the true cost from 6% to 8.06% — that gap is exactly what APR exists to reveal.

This page assumes fixed monthly payments, a fixed nominal rate, and a single upfront fee deducted from the amount received. It does not model variable rates, balloon payments, early-repayment penalties, ongoing monthly charges, or fees paid separately rather than deducted — each of those changes the APR. Lenders' disclosed APRs follow jurisdiction-specific rules about which charges count; this page's figure is a transparent calculation from the four inputs shown, not a lender disclosure. If fees are zero, APR equals the nominal rate (effective APR is slightly higher because of monthly compounding).

135/85: systolic 135 falls in 130–139 (Stage 1) and diastolic 85 falls in 80–89 (Stage 1), so the category is Stage 1 hypertension. Pulse pressure = 135 − 85 = 50 mmHg. A single reading does not diagnose hypertension — diagnosis rests on repeated readings over time, interpreted by a clinician.
Systolic is the pressure when the heart contracts; diastolic is the pressure between beats. Both matter — the category uses whichever falls in the higher band.
No. Diagnosis requires repeated elevated readings over time, usually including readings taken outside the clinic. A single high reading is a reason to recheck, not a diagnosis.
White-coat effect: stress in a clinical setting raises readings for many people. Home readings taken with correct technique are often lower and are part of the diagnostic picture.

Seated, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart height, correct cuff size, no caffeine or exercise in the prior 30 minutes, and a few minutes of rest first. Two readings a minute apart, averaged, beat one rushed reading.
The gap between systolic and diastolic — 50 mmHg in the example. A wide gap can reflect stiff arteries, but it is interpreted alongside the absolute numbers, not alone.

It does not distinguish muscle from fat, so it can misclassify very muscular or very slight builds, and it does not apply in the same way to children, whose categories use age- and sex-specific percentiles. Height and weight are taken as entered; no other personal circumstances are modelled.

Underweight is below 18.5, healthy weight is 18.5–24.9, overweight is 25.0–29.9, and obesity is 30.0 and above. These are the standard interval definitions, used here only as labels for the computed number.

BMI divided by 25, the top of the healthy range. A value of 1.00 sits exactly at that boundary; 0.95 is 5% below it.

Estimate resting energy expenditure with the Mifflin–St Jeor equation, from weight, height, age, and sex.
Bars are scaled to the larger of the two values. The only difference between the two bars is the sex constant (+5 for male, −161 for female) in the Mifflin–St Jeor equation.

BMR is resting expenditure only — it excludes activity, digestion, and exercise, so it is lower than total daily expenditure. The Mifflin–St Jeor equation is a population estimate: it was fitted to group averages, so individual results vary with body composition, illness, medications, and other factors the inputs do not capture. It is not a metabolic test and not a personal energy prescription.
The energy the body uses at complete rest to maintain basic functions. Any activity on top of rest adds to it, which is why total daily expenditure is higher.

The Mifflin–St Jeor equation adds +5 for men and subtracts 161 for women, reflecting average differences in the populations the equation was fitted to. It is a group adjustment, not a measurement of any individual.
No. Daily need also includes activity. Multiply BMR by an activity factor — or use the TDEE Calculator — for a total daily estimate.
It is an estimate from a population equation. Individual values can differ materially; only a metabolic test measures resting expenditure directly.
Yes, through the −5 × age term: each additional year lowers the estimate by 5 kcal/day at fixed weight and height.
Estimate body-fat percentage from BMI, age, and sex using the Deurenberg population equation.
Bars are scaled to the larger of the two values. The 10.8-point sex term is the only difference between the bars.

This is not a direct body-composition measurement: no skinfold, scan, or weighing method is involved, and the equation only recombines BMI, age, and sex. It can be inaccurate for athletes, older adults, and many body types, because two people with the same BMI and age can carry very different amounts of muscle and fat. The fat-mass and lean-mass figures are just the percentage applied to the entered weight, not separately measured quantities.
No. A scan or skinfold test measures the body directly; this page only applies a population equation to BMI, age, and sex.
The equation subtracts 10.8 points for men, reflecting average differences in the population it was fitted to. It is a group adjustment, not a measurement of the individual.
Because BMI cannot tell muscle from fat. A muscular person can have a high BMI — and therefore a high estimated body fat — while carrying little fat.
They are the estimated percentage applied to your entered weight (fat mass = weight × percentage; lean mass = the rest). They are not separately measured.
No. The equation is an adult population formula and is not validated for children.
Find the units and revenue needed for contribution margin to cover fixed costs.
Every unit sold beyond break-even adds one unit of contribution margin to profit, at these prices and costs.
Fixed costs and variable cost are held at the values above; only the price changes across rows.

Fixed costs $50,000, price $200, variable cost $120: contribution margin is $200 − $120 = $80 per unit, so break-even units = $50,000 ÷ $80 = 625 units, and break-even revenue = 625 × $200 = $125,000.

Price must exceed variable cost, or break-even never arrives. Product mix, taxes, stepped costs that jump at capacity limits, volume discounts, and changing prices are excluded — this is a single-product, constant-price model.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (unit price − unit variable cost). It finds the sales volume where total contribution exactly pays the fixed costs.
Then every sale loses money and there is no break-even volume — selling more only deepens the loss. The price must cover the variable cost before fixed costs can be recovered.
Price minus variable cost per unit: the amount each sale contributes toward fixed costs and then profit. Here it is $80 per unit at the example values.
No. Treat the break-even revenue as pre-tax revenue and apply your own tax treatment separately.
No. With a product mix you need a weighted-average contribution margin. This calculator models one product at one price.

A multiple of resting energy cost. Sitting quietly is 1 MET; an activity rated 6 MET is treated as costing six times as much energy per minute.
Because the MET figure is an average across people, and your efficiency, fitness, and equipment differ from that average.
Yes — the result is gross expenditure, which includes the energy you would have used at rest during those minutes.
The formula assumes one constant intensity. For mixed sessions, split the time by intensity and add the parts, or treat the result as an average-intensity approximation.

Area, circumference, and diameter of a circle from its radius, with the formulas shown and worked through.
Enter the radius in any unit — metres, centimetres, inches — and the results come back in that unit (square units for area). Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.
Area = π × radius². Circumference = 2 × π × radius. Diameter = 2 × radius. π is used at full precision and results are rounded to two decimals for display.
Radius 5: area = π × 5² = π × 25 = 78.54. Circumference = 2 × π × 5 = 31.42. Diameter = 10. If the radius was 5 cm, the area is 78.54 cm² and the circumference is 31.42 cm.

This is a perfect circle: one radius, one centre. Ellipses, arcs, sectors, and rings need their own formulas and are not covered here. The page does not convert units — a radius in inches gives an area in square inches; convert first if you need another unit.
Radius: the distance from the centre to the edge. If you only know the diameter (edge to edge through the centre), halve it first — or read the diameter chip above in reverse.
Because area covers a surface. A radius of 5 cm gives 78.54 cm², not 78.54 cm. Mixing the two is the most common circle mistake.
Full double-precision pi (3.141592653589793…), not 3.14. The difference only matters past the second decimal, but there is no reason to round early.
With the square: doubling the radius quadruples the area. A radius-10 circle has area 314.16, exactly four times the radius-5 area of 78.54.
No. A sphere's surface area is 4πr² and its volume is (4/3)πr³ — different formulas for a 3D object.
Divide it by 2π to get the radius, then enter that here. For a circumference of 31.42, the radius is 31.42 ÷ 6.2832 = 5.

Estimate the ROI of a piece of creator content from production cost, views, conversion, order value, and margin.
Revenue is orders times order value; gross profit applies the margin to revenue. ROI is net profit divided by production cost.
Bars are scaled to the larger of production cost and gross profit. Profit must clear the cost bar to be positive.
Each row reuses your conversion rate, order value, margin, and cost and varies only views, so you can find the view count that breaks even.

Cost $1,800, views 50,000, conversion 0.8%, order value $199, margin 55%. Orders = 50,000 × 0.8% = 400. Revenue = 400 × $199 = $79,600. Gross profit = $79,600 × 55% = $43,780. Net = $43,780 − $1,800 = $41,980. ROI = $41,980 ÷ $1,800 × 100% = 2,332.22%. Break-even views at these rates are about 2,056 views (cost divided by profit per view of $0.8756: 0.8% x $199 x 55%).

Views and conversion are your assumptions, not a traffic forecast; a view count does not guarantee that conversion rate, and past content is only a rough guide. Revenue alone is not profit — the margin input is doing that work, so an overstated margin overstates ROI directly. Attribution is not modeled: orders credited to the piece may have been influenced by other channels, and production cost here is a single figure, excluding distribution, promotion, and revision costs unless you include them in it.
Orders are views times the conversion rate; gross profit is orders times order value times margin; ROI is gross profit minus production cost, divided by production cost, times 100%.
A measured one from comparable past content with the same offer and audience, not a platform average. If you have no measured rate, run the page at several rates and see how far ROI moves.
Because revenue is not profit. Without margin, a high-revenue, low-margin product looks far better than it is. Enter the gross margin on the orders themselves, after product and fulfilment costs.

Everything spent making the piece: creator time or fees, editing, props, locations, and licences. Add paid promotion separately if you want it counted — either include it in the cost or run a second scenario.

Convert an amount at a rate you enter, less an optional fee — no market rate is fetched or implied.
The fee is taken from the converted amount. Enter the rate your provider actually quotes, not a rate from memory.
No rate is fetched from any market source. The default 7.2 is an example placeholder carried over from the original tool, labelled as such — it is not a quote, not current, and not a recommendation.
1,000 × 7.2 = 7,200 gross. A 1% fee is 7,200 × 0.01 = 72, so the amount received is 7,200 − 72 = 7,128. The effective rate is 7,128 ÷ 1,000 = 7.128 per unit.

This page does not provide a live or market exchange rate, and the default rate is an example only. Banks and payment providers add spreads and fixed fees that this single fee percentage may not capture; confirm the actual rate, spread, and any fixed charge before sending money. Display values are rounded to 6 decimal places; real providers round to the currency's smallest unit, which can change the final cents.
No. It is an example value (7.2) carried over from the original tool, clearly labelled as an example. This page fetches no market data — always replace it with a rate your provider quotes.
Only if you fold the spread into the fee percentage yourself. A provider quoting a worse rate than the market is charging you a hidden spread on top of any stated fee.
Subtract it from the gross yourself: received = amount × rate − fixed fee. This page models percentage fees only.
Because the fee percentage is deducted from the converted amount. With a 0% fee the two are equal.
Yes: divide instead of multiplying. If 1,000 units buy 7,128 at the example rate and fee, the reverse effective rate is 1,000 ÷ 7,128 = 0.140292 per unit.
All five units describe the same amount of data under the base you selected; switching the base changes every row.

Strictly, KiB/MiB/GiB are the base-1024 units and KB/MB/GB are base-1000 SI units. In practice many operating systems label base-1024 sizes as KB/MB/GB; this page follows that common labelling and lets you switch base explicitly instead of hiding the difference.

Negative sizes are rejected as invalid. Display values are rounded to 6 decimal places; the underlying calculation is not rounded. Formatted drive capacity, filesystem overhead, and the KiB-vs-KB naming dispute are not modelled — this page converts the number you enter, nothing more.

Use 1000 for SI/manufacturer specifications (a drive sold as 1 TB usually means 10^12 bytes) and 1024 for the sizes most operating systems report. When in doubt, check which one your source used — the gap reaches about 10% at TB scale.
GiB is unambiguously base 1024 (1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes); GB is the SI base-1000 unit. Many tools write GB when they mean GiB, which is why this page makes the base an explicit choice.
Partly this base difference: 10^12 bytes = 931.32 GiB at base 1024. Filesystem overhead accounts for the rest.
1,024 MB at base 1024, or 1,000 MB at base 1000 — the answer depends on the base, so always state it.
The headline count excludes the end date (1 January to 2 January is 1 day). Add 1 for the inclusive count, which counts both endpoints.

Calendar difference = end date − start date, evaluated using local calendar dates. The years–months–days breakdown counts completed calendar years, then completed months, then remaining days, in the same way as an age calculation.

From 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2026: 364 days, exactly 52 weeks, and a calendar breakdown of 11 months and 30 days. The inclusive count, counting both 1 January and 31 December, is 365 days. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result.

Only whole local calendar dates are compared; times of day and time zones are ignored. Leap years are handled by the calendar itself — 2026 is not a leap year, while an interval spanning 29 February 2028 would include that day. Month lengths differ, so the years–months–days breakdown is a calendar statement, not days divided by 30. No public holidays are involved in this count; for weekdays only, use the workday calculator.
No, in the headline count. From 1 January to 2 January is 1 day. The inclusive count (both endpoints) is shown separately and is always one more.
Because months are 28–31 days long. Dividing by 30 gives an approximation that drifts; the calendar breakdown here counts completed months exactly.
By the real calendar. A 29 February falling inside the interval adds one day to the count automatically.
The day count is negative and the page flags it. The calendar breakdown is then shown for the interval in the other direction, labelled as such.
No. It counts calendar days only. To exclude weekends, use the workday calculator.
Estimate the annual cost of digital clutter: monthly storage fees plus the value of time spent searching for things, and how fast a cleanup could pay for itself.
Bars are scaled to the larger component. Search time is an opportunity cost valued at your hourly figure, not cash you pay out.
Same storage fee and hourly value; only the weekly search minutes change.

Monthly storage 68, 45 search minutes per week, hourly value 80, cleanup 6 hours: storage = 68 × 12 = 816.00; search time = 45 ÷ 60 × 52 = 39 hours per year, valued at 39 × 80 = 3,120.00; annual cost = 816.00 + 3,120.00 = 3,936.00. Cleanup value = 6 × 80 = 480.00; monthly average = 3,936.00 ÷ 12 = 328.00; payback = 480.00 ÷ 328.00 = 1.46 months. These are example inputs — your hourly value is a judgement, not a market rate.

Search time is an opportunity cost, and the model does not prove cleanup will eliminate it: a cleanup may reduce search time without removing it, and the payback figure assumes the full monthly average is recovered. Storage fees are cash costs; search-time value is not cash unless the freed time is actually used productively. Your hourly value should reflect what your time is worth to you, not a wage claim.

Calculate the final price and total savings after percentage and fixed discounts.
The fixed discount is applied after the percentage discount, and the final price is floored at zero — it can never go negative.
The two bars together equal the original price. A larger saving bar means a deeper effective discount.
Original price and extra discount are held at the values above; only the percentage discount changes across rows.
Original price $100, discount 20%, extra discount $5: final price = $100 × (1 − 0.20) − $5 = $80 − $5 = $75, so you save $25, an effective 25.00% off.

Tax, shipping, minimum-spend rules, coupon order, and exclusions may change the checkout total. If a store applies the fixed discount before the percentage discount, the result differs slightly — this calculator applies the percentage first, as stated in the formula.
Final price = original price × (1 − discount rate) − additional fixed discount, floored at zero. The percentage comes off first, then the fixed amount.
Percentage first, then the fixed discount. Reversing the order changes the result when both are present, so check the store's order if the total differs by a small amount.
No. If the discounts exceed the price, the result is floored at $0.00 and the saving is capped at the original price.
Total saving divided by the original price. With a 20% discount plus $5 off $100, the effective saving is 25%, not 20%.
Not modeled. If the discount only applies above a spend threshold or excludes some items, the checkout total will differ.
Compare a loan's payoff time and interest before and after adding extra monthly principal.
Bars are scaled to the larger interest total. Extra principal saves interest twice over: less balance accrues interest, and the loan ends sooner.
Each month, interest is balance times annual rate divided by 12, then the payment (plus extra, where applicable) reduces the balance. The final payment is capped at what remains.

Each month: interest = opening balance × annual rate ÷ 12; payment reduces the balance after interest. The simulation repeats until the balance reaches zero, once with the scheduled payment and once with the payment plus extra principal.

Balance $200,000 at 3.5% with a $1,500 payment: payoff in 170 months with $53,642.99 of interest. Adding $200 a month ($1,700 total) pays off in 145 months with $45,320.90 of interest — 25 months sooner and $8,322.09 less interest.

Fixed rate, fixed payments made on time, extra payments applied to principal with no prepayment penalty and no fees. If the scheduled payment does not cover monthly interest, the balance grows and the loan never pays off on that payment; the calculator flags that case.
It cuts the balance every month, so every later month accrues interest on a smaller amount. The effect compounds over the life of the loan.
Then the balance grows instead of shrinking, and the loan never pays off at that payment. Raise the payment above the first month's interest to make progress.
It depends on the rate. Extra payments help at any rate; refinancing helps when a lower rate is available. Compare both with the refinance calculator.
Here, yes, in full, in the month it is paid. Some lenders apply extra payments differently; check how yours treats them.
Not modeled here. A lump sum has a similar effect — it cuts the balance at once — but the timing changes the saving.
Estimate appliance energy use and cost from wattage, hours per day, days, quantity, and the electricity rate you enter.
Bars are scaled to the larger cost. The full-year bar assumes the same daily use every day; it is a projection, not a bill forecast.
Same wattage, hours, rate and quantity; only the number of days changes. The rate you enter is used throughout — tiered or time-of-use pricing is not modelled.

Power 1,500 W, 4 hours per day, 30 days, 1 device, rate 0.80 per kWh (an example rate you replace with your own): daily energy = 1,500 ÷ 1,000 × 4 = 6 kWh, so period energy = 6 × 30 = 180 kWh and cost = 180.00 × 0.80 = 144.00. Daily cost is 4.80. The rate here is only the example default — your bill's actual rate is what matters.

Standby power, duty cycles (appliances that cycle on and off), tiered rates, taxes, demand charges and time-of-use pricing are not modelled: a single flat rate is applied to all energy. If your appliance cycles, enter its average power draw, not its peak wattage. No rate is presented as a market average — the default rate is an example to replace.
Cost = watts ÷ 1,000 × hours per day × days × device count × price per kWh. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is 1,000 watts used for one hour.
The per-kWh price from your own bill or tariff, including only what you want the estimate to cover. If your bill adds taxes or fixed charges separately, this estimate will not match the bill total.
Standby draw is not included unless you add it: either add standby watts to the power input for the hours the device is plugged in, or run a second calculation for standby use.
Its average draw over the hours you enter, not the peak wattage on the label. A fridge rated at 150 W may average far less across a day.
Tiered rates, time-of-use pricing, fixed daily charges, taxes and other appliances on the same bill all sit outside this single-appliance calculation.
Estimate how many months your cash covers essential spending when income drops.
Bars are scaled to total cash. The buffer is money you choose not to spend even in an emergency; usable cash is what actually funds the runway.
Each row recomputes usable cash as cash times (1 minus buffer) and divides by the same monthly shortfall.

Monthly shortfall = monthly expenses − monthly emergency income. Usable cash = cash × (1 − buffer%). Runway = usable cash ÷ monthly shortfall, when the shortfall is positive. If income covers expenses, the runway is not limited by cash.
Cash $120,000 with a 10% buffer: usable cash is $120,000 × 90% = $108,000, kept back $12,000. Monthly shortfall is $15,000 − $5,000 = $10,000, so runway is $108,000 ÷ $10,000 = 10.8 months.

Expenses and emergency income are assumed flat every month, with no interest earned on cash, no new debts, no one-off costs, and no change in the buffer. Real emergencies are lumpy: a single large bill shortens the runway more than the smooth monthly average suggests.
Money you deliberately do not spend: a floor for non-negotiable costs, a deposit, or a reserve for the month after the emergency. A larger buffer shortens the runway but leaves a cushion.
Then the shortfall is zero or negative and cash is not being drained: the runway is not limited by cash on these figures. The calculator says so rather than dividing by zero.
Bare-minimum essential spending gives the true emergency runway. Normal spending gives a shorter, more conservative figure; run both and compare.
Not here. Interest on a cash pile is small relative to monthly spending, and assuming none keeps the estimate conservative.

That depends on your situation and is not a number this calculator prescribes. Common planning horizons are a few months to a year; the sensitivity table above shows what each buffer level costs in months.
Add, subtract, multiply or divide two fractions and reduce the result.

Add: a/b + c/d = (ad + bc) / bd. Subtract: a/b − c/d = (ad − bc) / bd. Multiply: a/b × c/d = ac / bd. Divide: a/b ÷ c/d = ad / bc. In every case, divide the resulting numerator and denominator by their greatest common divisor (GCD) to simplify, keeping any minus sign in the numerator.

1/2 + 1/3 = (1×3 + 1×2) / (2×3) = 5/6. The GCD of 5 and 6 is 1, so 5/6 is already simplest, and its decimal value is 0.833333… (shown as 0.8333). Use Reset example above to reproduce this result, then replace the values with your own.

Inputs may be whole numbers, negatives, or finite decimals. Decimal values are converted to base-10 fractions before exact integer arithmetic and simplification. The browser reads inputs as JavaScript numbers, so digits beyond its numeric precision cannot be recovered. Denominators must not be zero, and division also requires a nonzero second numerator. Results are rounded to 4 decimal places for display only; the underlying fraction is exact for integer inputs.
The result is not shown. A fraction with a zero denominator is undefined, so the page asks for a nonzero denominator instead of inventing a number.
By the greatest common divisor: for example 4/6 divides by GCD 2 to give 2/3. The sign is kept in the numerator, so −1/2 and 1/−2 both display as −1/2.
Fractions such as 1/3 have no exact finite decimal. The decimal shown is rounded to 4 places (0.3333); the fraction itself, 1/3, is the exact answer.
Yes. Enter a negative numerator (or denominator); the result is normalised so the denominator stays positive.
A whole part plus a fraction, for example 7/3 = 2 1/3. It is shown for improper results; proper fractions and whole numbers are shown as they are.

Estimate trip fuel expense from distance, fuel economy, the fuel price you enter, and tolls and parking.
Bars are scaled to the larger of the two costs. Tolls and parking are entered as one combined figure.
Same fuel economy and fuel price, with the same tolls and parking figure at every distance, so the fuel component is what changes.

Distance 500 km, economy 7.5 L/100 km, price 8 per litre, tolls and parking 100: fuel used = 500 ÷ 100 × 7.5 = 37.5 L, fuel cost = 37.50 × 8 = 300.00, trip cost = 300.00 + 100 = 400.00, or 0.80 per km. The fuel price here is only the example default — enter the price you actually expect to pay.

Vehicle depreciation, maintenance, insurance, traffic, elevation and fuel-price changes along the route are excluded. Fuel economy is treated as constant, although real consumption varies with speed, load, weather and driving style. Tolls and parking are a single combined input: add both together before entering. No fuel price is presented as a market average.
The price you expect to pay on the route, in the same currency as the result you want. Prices vary by station and region, so the example default is only a placeholder.
Double the distance before entering it, or run the calculation once and double the fuel component. Tolls and parking for the return leg go in the same combined field.
Economy figures are usually measured in standard conditions. City traffic, heavy loads, roof boxes, cold weather and high speeds all raise consumption.
No. This is a liquid-fuel calculation in litres per 100 km. An EV needs an energy-consumption figure in kWh per 100 km and an electricity price instead.
US MPG uses US gallons (3.785411784 L); UK MPG uses imperial gallons (4.54609 L) — the UK figure is always higher for the same car.
Bars are scaled to the 600 km trip. Fuel for a trip = rate (L/100km) × trip distance ÷ 100.

L/100 km = litres ÷ kilometres × 100. US MPG converts kilometres and litres to miles and US gallons: MPG (US) = (km ÷ 1.609344) ÷ (L ÷ 3.785411784). UK MPG uses 4.54609 L per gallon instead. Km/L = kilometres ÷ litres.

A single tank-to-tank figure is noisy: fill level, route, weather, load, and driving style all move it. Use fuel added over a comparable full-tank interval, as the source tool advised, and average several tanks for a reliable figure. Manufacturer figures are measured on test cycles and usually beat real-world results. Display values are rounded to 6 decimal places.
Roughly: under 6 is economical, 6–9 is mid-range for a family petrol car, above 9 is thirsty. Diesels, hybrids, and electric cars are not directly comparable on this scale.
Same car, bigger gallon: an imperial gallon (4.54609 L) holds about 20% more fuel than a US gallon (3.785411784 L), so the same distance per litre reads higher in UK MPG.
US MPG = 235.214583 ÷ L/100km. For 7.5 L/100km that gives 31.361944, matching the worked example.
Several. One tank is easily skewed by how full the pump stops. Average over at least three comparable fill-ups.
No — this page measures consumption only. The fuel-cost calculator (linked below) turns consumption into money.

= $16,288.95. Interest earned is $16,288.95 − $10,000 = $6,288.95, and the growth multiple is 1.63×. After 5 years the same sum is worth $12,762.82.

Yes, but less than rate and time. Monthly compounding on the example gives $16,470.09 instead of $16,288.95 — about $181 more over 10 years. Daily compounding adds only a little more again.
None in the math: compound interest is the interest earned, future value is the total. This page shows both so you do not have to subtract by hand.
Yes. At 0% the future value equals the present value and no interest is earned.
No. To compare purchasing power, divide the future value by (1 + inflation rate)
They are not included here. A lump sum plus deposits needs the future value of an annuity added on top — a separate calculation with its own formula.
Because growth compounds: each year's interest earns interest in later years. Over 30 years, 6% instead of 5% on $10,000 gives $57,434.91 instead of $43,219.42.

Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold only — operating expenses are not deducted here.

Gross profit = revenue − cost of goods sold. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100%. COGS ratio = cost of goods sold ÷ revenue × 100%.
Revenue $100,000, cost of goods sold $60,000: gross profit = $100,000 − $60,000 = $40,000, gross margin = $40,000 ÷ $100,000 × 100% = 40.00%, and COGS ratio = 60.00%.

Gross profit = revenue − cost of goods sold; gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100%. It measures what is left after the direct cost of what you sold.
Net margin deducts everything, including operating expenses, interest, and tax. Gross margin stops at cost of goods sold, so it is higher and says nothing about overhead.
Yes, if cost of goods sold exceeds revenue — each sale loses money before any operating cost is even counted. That needs a price or sourcing fix, not cost-cutting elsewhere.
Direct costs of producing or buying what you sold: materials, direct labor, and wholesale purchase cost. Rent and marketing are operating expenses, not COGS.
Because COGS is held fixed in the scenario table. In reality COGS usually rises with volume, so read that table as a what-if, not a forecast.
Generally, but not at any price: raising prices to lift margin can cut volume enough to reduce total gross profit. Margin percent and total profit must be read together.
Turn a daily habit into total hours: minutes per day, planned days, completion rate, and the workday length you use for comparison.
Bars are scaled to the scheduled total. Missed hours are the scheduled hours you did not complete at the completion rate you enter.
Same minutes per day and completion rate; only the number of days changes. The final row is the full planned period.
Total practice hours = daily minutes ÷ 60 × planned days × completion%. Equivalent workdays = total practice hours ÷ workday length.

30 minutes per day, 365 planned days, 80% completion, 8-hour workday: scheduled hours = 30 ÷ 60 × 365 = 182.5 hours; completed hours = 182.5 × 0.80 = 146 hours; missed hours = 182.5 − 146 = 36.5 hours; equivalent workdays = 146.00 ÷ 8 = 18.25 days. These are example inputs — completion is your own estimate, not a measured rate.

Equivalent workdays divide hours by the entered day length; they are a scale comparison, not a claim about output. Time accumulated does not establish learning quality, mastery or compound performance gains: an hour of focused practice and an hour of distracted repetition count the same here. Completion is treated as a flat rate across the whole period, so streaks, breaks and improving consistency are not modelled.
The share of planned days you actually do the habit, averaged over the whole period. 80% over 365 days means about 292 days completed, not any particular pattern of streaks and breaks.
Not necessarily. Time accumulated does not establish learning quality, mastery or compound performance gains — how you practise matters as much as how long.
A scale comparison: total hours divided by the workday length you enter. 146 hours is 18.25 eight-hour days, which is easier to picture than a raw hour count.
Convert it to a daily average first: for example, 3 sessions of 60 minutes a week averages about 25.7 minutes per day (180 ÷ 7).

Estimate how many months of expected extra income it takes to repay tuition plus the value of study time.
Expected monthly gain already includes the probability adjustment: a $2,500 gain at 60% counts as $1,500 per month.
Bars compare the full investment with the expected gain over the first 12 months. If the gain bar is shorter, payback runs beyond a year.
Each row is expected cumulative gain minus the full investment, assuming the monthly gain starts immediately and stays constant. A delayed start pushes every row later.

Payback months = (tuition + learning hours × hourly value) ÷ (expected monthly raise × probability%). Expected monthly benefit = expected monthly raise × probability%. Net after N months = expected monthly benefit × N − total investment.

Tuition $12,000, 160 hours at $60, expected monthly gain $2,500 at 60% probability. Total investment = $12,000 + 160 × $60 = $21,600. Expected monthly benefit = $2,500 × 60% = $1,500. Payback = $21,600 ÷ $1,500 = 14.4 months. Net after 12 months = $1,500 × 12 − $21,600 = −$3,600; after 24 months = $1,500 × 24 − $21,600 = $14,400.

Expected income and probability are assumptions, not measured outcomes: a course provider's placement figure is not your probability. A zero expected monthly benefit has no finite financial payback, and the model assumes the gain starts immediately and never changes — real gains are delayed, partial, and may fade. Non-financial benefits (enjoyment, mobility, option value) are real but are not counted here, and neither are taxes on extra income, exam or material fees beyond the tuition input, or the risk of not completing the course.
Total investment (tuition plus study hours times hourly value) divided by the expected monthly benefit, which is the expected monthly raise times its probability.
Because hours spent learning have an opportunity cost. Ignoring them flatters expensive, time-heavy courses; valuing them at your hourly rate keeps the comparison honest.

Your honest estimate that you achieve the stated gain, given your background and the local market — not a provider's headline rate. Run the page at half your first guess to see how sensitive payback is.
Add those months to the payback figure. The model assumes income starts at once; a six-month job search turns a 14.4-month payback into roughly 20.4 months from enrolment.

No. Satisfaction, career mobility, and the option to change fields are excluded. A course can fail this financial test and still be worth doing — but that should be a conscious choice, not an accident of the maths.
Because dividing by zero has no finite answer. If the expected gain is genuinely zero, the investment is never repaid by income, whatever its other merits.

For ax + b = 0 with a ≠ 0: x = −b ÷ a. For a line in slope-intercept form y = mx + c: the slope is m (rise over run), the y-intercept is c (the value at x = 0), and the x-intercept is −c ÷ m (the x value where y = 0, when m ≠ 0). If a = 0, the equation ax + b = 0 has no solution unless b is also 0, in which case every x is a solution.

3x + 6 = 0: x = −6 ÷ 3 = −2. Check: 3 × (−2) + 6 = 0. For the line y = 2x + 3: the slope is 2 (y rises 2 for each 1 step in x), the y-intercept is 3, and the x-intercept is −3 ÷ 2 = −1.50. The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 3) and the x-axis at (−1.50, 0).

This page solves single linear equations in one variable and describes straight lines. It does not solve quadratics (see the quadratic equation calculator), systems of equations (see the system of equations calculator), or inequalities — though the x-intercept of y = mx + c does tell you where the sign of mx + c changes. Inputs are plain numbers; fractions must be entered as decimals, and very large or tiny coefficients may lose precision in display, though the underlying arithmetic is standard double precision.

Then the equation is b = 0, which does not involve x. If b is also 0, every value of x satisfies it (the equation is an identity). If b is not 0, no value of x satisfies it. The page says which case applies instead of dividing by zero.
Rise over run: how much y changes when x increases by 1. A slope of 2 means y climbs 2 per x step; a slope of −0.5 means y falls half a unit per x step. A slope of 0 is a horizontal line.

It is where the line crosses the x-axis, i.e. where y = 0. For y = 2x + 3, solving 2x + 3 = 0 gives x = −1.50 — the same calculation as the equation solver, which is no coincidence: intercepts are just solutions of the equation.
Enter them as decimals (1/2 as 0.5). The page shows results to two decimals; repeating decimals such as 1/3 display as 0.33, so for exact fractional work keep the fraction form alongside.

Slope-intercept form y = mx + c exposes the slope and y-intercept directly. Standard form Ax + By = C is the same line rearranged: m = −A ÷ B and c = C ÷ B (when B ≠ 0). This page works in slope-intercept form.
Substituting the solution back catches sign errors, the most common mistake in linear equations. For 3x + 6 = 0, x = −2 checks out because 3(−2) + 6 = 0; x = 2 would give 12, not 0.

Central tendency of a data set: mean, median, and mode, with the sorted data, sum, count, and range shown alongside.

Mean = sum of all values ÷ count. Median = the middle value of the sorted data (or the average of the two middle values when the count is even). Mode = the value that appears most often; a data set can have several modes, or none when every value appears once.

Data 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 8, 9: sorted, that is 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 8, 9. Sum = 43, count = 7, so mean = 43 ÷ 7 = 6.14. The middle (4th) value is 6, so the median is 6. The value 8 appears twice — more than any other — so the mode is 8. Range = 9 − 3 = 6.

These are descriptive measures of the data you enter — they describe this set, not a wider population, and they say nothing about spread on their own (pair them with range or standard deviation for that). The mean is pulled by outliers: one very large value raises it even when most values are small, which is exactly when the median is the better summary. Modes are only meaningful for data where repeats are expected; with continuous measurements, exact repeats are rare and the mode may not exist.

Report the mean for roughly symmetric data and the median when the data is skewed or has outliers. Income is the classic case: a few very high incomes raise the mean well above what a typical person earns, so median income is the standard headline figure.
With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values. For 2, 4, 7, 9 the median is (4 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5.50.
Yes. If two values tie for the highest frequency, the data is bimodal and both are modes. This page lists all tied values.
Every value appears exactly once, so nothing is most frequent. That is common with continuous measurements like heights recorded to the millimetre.
No. Sorting is done for you; the median and the sorted list are computed from whatever order you paste in.
No. Commas, spaces, and line breaks all work as separators, so pasted spreadsheet columns work directly.
Annual time value of a recurring meeting from people, hourly cost, length and frequency.
Person-hours = people × minutes ÷ 60, scaled by meetings per week and working weeks.

Annual time value = people × hourly cost × meeting minutes ÷ 60 × weekly meetings × working weeks. Cost per meeting = people × hourly cost × minutes ÷ 60. Cost per week = cost per meeting × weekly meetings.

9 people at $180/hour for 60 minutes: cost per meeting = 9 × 180 × 60 ÷ 60 = $1,620. At 3 meetings per week that is $4,860 per week, and over 48 working weeks the annual time value is $1,620 × 3 × 48 = $233,280, or 1,296 person-hours per year. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result.

This is an opportunity-cost estimate based on the average hourly cost you enter, not necessarily an avoidable cash expense: salaried staff are paid whether or not they attend. Preparation time is included only if you add it to the meeting length. Room, tooling, and travel costs are not included. The hourly figure should be a fully loaded cost (salary plus on-costs) if the result is meant to represent total staff cost.
Not necessarily. It is the value of staff time freed up. Cash is saved only if that time would otherwise be paid overtime or contractor time.
Yes, if you want total staff cost. Use a fully loaded rate — salary plus benefits, payroll taxes and overhead — rather than base pay alone.
Add it to the meeting length, or run a second calculation for preparation and add the two results.
It is the example assumption (52 weeks less holidays and leave). Change it to match your own calendar.
In this model, yes: cost scales linearly with minutes, people, and frequency, so halving any one of them halves the cost.
Mass of one mole of a compound from its chemical formula — with the elemental composition alongside.
Element symbols with counts; parentheses allowed, e.g. Ca(OH)2. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.
The number after a closing parenthesis multiplies everything inside it. In Ca(OH)2, the 2 doubles both O and H: Ca + O2 + H2, giving 40.078 + 2 × 15.999 + 2 × 1.008 = 74.092 g/mol.
To convert mass to moles, divide grams by molar mass; to convert moles to mass, multiply. For example, 36.03 g of water is 36.03 ÷ 18.015 = 2.00 moles.
Numerically yes, units differ: molecular weight is a relative number (unitless), molar mass is that number expressed in g/mol. People use the terms interchangeably in most contexts.

Loan = home price − down payment. Loan-to-value = loan ÷ home price. Principal & interest uses the standard amortization formula on the loan amount. PMI applies only when loan-to-value exceeds 80%, at loan × PMI rate ÷ 12 per month. Tax and insurance are annual figures ÷ 12.

Home price $400,000 with $80,000 down: loan $320,000, loan-to-value 80.00%. At 6.5% for 30 years, principal & interest is $2,022.62. Add tax $400.00 and insurance $125.00 a month; PMI is $0 because loan-to-value does not exceed 80%. Total monthly payment $2,547.62.

Fixed rate for the whole term, PMI charged at a flat rate while loan-to-value exceeds 80% (real PMI usually drops off and is repriced), and no closing costs, points, or rate adjustments. Tax and insurance are assumed constant; in practice both change over time. Extra principal shortens the loan but is not included in the headline total above.
Here, only when the loan exceeds 80% of the home price. At exactly 80% there is no PMI in this model. Lenders also apply their own PMI rules and cancellation thresholds.
No. The headline total is the required monthly bill. Extra principal is voluntary and is shown separately so the required payment stays comparable.

Estimate take-home pay from gross income, an effective tax rate you enter, and deductions.
All figures are monthly unless labeled per year. The tax rate is an effective rate you enter — it is not any jurisdiction's statutory rate.
Net pay plus deductions equals gross pay. A longer deductions bar means less than half of gross pay reaches you.
Gross pay and other deductions are held at the values above; only the tax rate changes across rows.
Estimated tax = gross pay × effective tax rate. Net pay = gross pay − estimated tax − social contributions − other deductions. Net pay per year = net pay per month × 12.

Gross pay $6,000 per month, effective tax rate 15%, social contributions $500, other deductions $0: estimated tax = $6,000 × 0.15 = $900, net pay = $6,000 − $900 − $500 − $0 = $4,600 per month, or $55,200 per year.

Tax systems vary by location and personal circumstances: brackets, allowances, credits, employer contributions, and benefits are not modeled. Enter an effective rate from your own payslip or payroll calculation and verify important figures against an official payroll calculation. This is an estimate, not a payroll or tax filing.
Net pay = gross pay − estimated tax − social contributions − other deductions, where estimated tax = gross pay × the effective tax rate you enter.

Your actual tax divided by your gross pay from a recent payslip, or a rate your payroll department confirms. No country or region's rate is pre-filled, because statutory rates and brackets differ too much to assume.
Deductions exceed gross pay at the values entered. Check the rate and deduction amounts — a negative result flags an input problem, not a real payslip.
No. Only deductions from your gross pay are counted. Employer-side contributions are a separate cost and do not reduce your net pay here.
Only if you fold them into the monthly gross pay you enter. Irregular pay should be averaged or calculated for the specific month.
No. It is a take-home estimate. Filing depends on your jurisdiction's full rules, allowances, and credits.
Solve any variable of Ohm's law — voltage, current, resistance, or power — from the other two, with power shown alongside.
The two input labels change with the chosen unknown. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

V = I × R, and P = V × I. From those two, every other form follows: I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I, P = I² × R, P = V² ÷ R. The "Check" chip recomputes the solved value through the other relation to confirm consistency.
Solve for current with V = 12 V and R = 4 Ω: I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 4 = 3.00 A. Power = V × I = 12 × 3 = 36.00 W. Check through the other form: P = V² ÷ R = 144 ÷ 4 = 36.00 W — consistent.

This is DC and resistive AC: it assumes voltage and current are in phase and resistance is constant. It does not cover reactive AC circuits (inductors, capacitors, phase shift) or temperature-dependent resistance — a filament lamp's resistance rises sharply as it heats, so cold resistance gives a misleading current. Zero resistance means a short circuit: current is unbounded in the ideal model, so the page refuses division by zero rather than showing infinity. Real circuits always have some resistance and a supply with a current limit.
Any two of voltage, current, and resistance determine the third — and power follows from any voltage-current pair. Pick the unknown above and enter the two you know.
Because I = V ÷ R with R = 0 is a short circuit: the ideal model predicts infinite current. Real supplies limit current or fail; no finite answer exists, so the page says so.
For resistive loads (heaters, incandescent lamps) yes, using RMS voltage and current. For motors and electronics with inductance or capacitance, use impedance and phase-aware calculations instead.
A resistor converts power to heat. A 36 W result through a 0.25 W resistor would destroy it — always check the component's power rating against the computed power, not just the resistance value.
Base SI units here: volts, amps, ohms, watts. For milliamps, divide by 1,000 first (500 mA = 0.5 A); for kilohms, multiply by 1,000 (4.7 kΩ = 4700 Ω).
Yes: choose Power and enter voltage and current. The page also shows the implied resistance (V ÷ I) as the check value.
Pace per kilometre, pace per mile, and average speed from race distance and finish time.
Pace bars are labels, not comparisons: a mile is longer than a kilometre, so the per-mile time is always larger at the same speed.
Total time = hours × 3,600 + minutes × 60 + seconds. Pace per kilometre = total time ÷ distance (km). Pace per mile = pace per kilometre × 1.609344. Speed = distance ÷ total hours.
Distance 10 km, finish time 50 minutes (3,000 seconds): pace = 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300 seconds =
(7.46 mph). At the same pace, 5 km takes 25:00 and a marathon takes 3:30:59. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result.

The result is a single average over the whole distance: it assumes perfectly even pacing and ignores pauses, terrain, weather, elevation, and GPS measurement error, all of which make real splits vary. Projected times for other distances assume the same pace can be held, which becomes less realistic as distance grows.
Because a mile (1.609344 km) is longer than a kilometre, so it takes proportionally longer at the same speed.
No. It divides total elapsed time by distance, so pauses and terrain are averaged into the single pace figure.
Only as an arithmetic projection: holding a 10 km pace for 42.195 km is much harder than holding it for 10 km, so treat projections as reference numbers.
Enter them as minutes instead — the seconds field is capped at 59, matching how times are normally written.
Convert first: divide miles by 0.621371 to get kilometres, or multiply kilometres by 0.621371 to go the other way.
Estimate paint volume from surface area, coats, coverage per litre, and a waste allowance you choose.
Bars are scaled to the larger of the two amounts. Waste is the extra paint on top of the exact coats calculation.
Paint per coat = area ÷ coverage per litre. Paint for all coats = area × coats ÷ coverage per litre. Paint required = paint for all coats × (1 + waste rate).

Area 120 m², 2 coats, coverage 10 m²/L: paint per coat = 120 ÷ 10 = 12 L, so 2 coats need 24 L. At a 10% waste allowance, waste = 24 × 0.10 = 2.4 L, giving 26.4 L required. These are the example defaults above; replace them with your own area and the coverage printed on your paint.

Coverage varies with surface porosity, primer, application method (brush, roller, spray), colour change and the manufacturer's stated rate — the coverage you enter should come from your paint's own data sheet. Doors, windows and trim must be subtracted from the area yourself if you do not intend to paint them. No can size or price is assumed: divide the result by your can size to get the number of cans.
Paint required = area × coats ÷ coverage per litre × (1 + waste rate). Every input is yours; nothing here is a market average.
Only if the primer is the same product at the same coverage. Otherwise calculate primer separately with its own coverage rate.
Porous or unprimed surfaces absorb more paint, dark-to-light colour changes need more coats, and spray application loses more to overspray than a roller does.
Divide the required litres by the size of the can you buy and round up. Can sizes differ by product and region, so no can size is built into this page.
Yes, if you are not painting them. Measure the wall area, then subtract the area of openings you will leave unpainted.
Percentage of base = base value × percentage ÷ 100. Value after increase = base × (1 + percentage ÷ 100). Value after decrease = base × (1 − percentage ÷ 100).
15% of 280 = 280 × 15 ÷ 100 = 42. After a 15% increase: 280 + 42 = 322. After a 15% decrease: 280 − 42 = 238. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result, then replace the values with your own.

Percentages may be negative or above 100; a decrease larger than 100% gives a negative result, which is arithmetically correct but may not be meaningful for the quantity being described. Results are rounded to 2 decimal places for display. This page computes percentages only — it does not add tax, fees, or compounding unless those are part of the percentage you enter.
Multiply the base by the percentage and divide by 100. For example, 15% of 280 is 280 × 15 ÷ 100 = 42.
The base plus the percentage amount: 280 increased by 15% is 280 + 42 = 322.
Yes. 150% of 280 is 420, and a 150% increase gives 700. The arithmetic is the same; check whether that makes sense for your situation.
A negative percentage reverses the direction: −15% of 280 is −42, so an 'increase' of −15% is really a decrease to 238.
Display is rounded to 2 decimal places. The underlying multiplication is not rounded before the increase and decrease figures are computed.

Bars are scaled to the larger figure. The reserve is a separate lump sum you set aside; it is not spread across years.
Cumulative figures include the reserve from the start, so the final row equals the lifetime budget. Cost growth compounds each year at the rate you enter.
− 1) ÷ r + reserve. With zero growth, use annual cost × n + reserve. Remaining years n = expected lifespan − current age.
Age 4, expected lifespan 14 (10 remaining years), annual cost 9,000, growth 4%, reserve 15,000: growth-adjusted costs = 9,000 × ((1.04
− 1) ÷ 0.04) = 108,054.96, plus the 15,000 reserve = 123,054.96. All figures here are example inputs, not veterinary or market data — replace them with your own costs.

This is a nominal budget using an assumed lifespan and constant cost growth, not a veterinary or insurance estimate. It excludes nothing by name, but it only contains what you put in: if insurance, food, routine care and emergencies are not inside your annual cost or reserve, they are not in the result either. Lifespan is uncertain; test shorter and longer lifespans. Remaining years cannot be negative.
Whatever you intend it to cover — typically emergencies or end-of-life care. It is a lump sum added once, not an annual amount.
Anything not inside your annual cost or reserve. It is not a veterinary quote and not an insurance estimate; it is a budgeting model built from your assumptions.
Because it compounds: at 4% over 10 years the growth-adjusted total (108,054.96) is well above 10 flat years at 9,000 (90,000). Small rate changes compound into large differences.
The budget rises with every extra year. Run the calculation at a longer lifespan as a sensitivity check, not just the central estimate.
pH from hydrogen ion concentration, with pOH, hydroxide concentration, and the acid–base label for the result.
Enter a concentration above zero, in moles per litre — 0.0001 means 10
mol/L. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.
Because concentrations span many orders of magnitude: stomach acid at pH 2 has 10,000 times the hydrogen ions of a pH 6 solution, not three times. Each whole pH step means a tenfold change.
Only at 25 °C. Neutral means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], and that balance point moves with temperature, so neutral water at 100 °C has pH 6.14.
Yes, for very concentrated acids or bases — a 10 mol/L strong acid has a nominal pH of −1. The 0–14 range is a rule of thumb for dilute solutions, not a law.

Meters measure activity, not concentration; temperature, calibration, and dissolved salts all shift readings. For weak acids, incomplete dissociation is usually the bigger cause — the concentration you put in is not the free [H⁺].
Pure water pH 7, coffee about 5, vinegar about 2.4, baking soda solution about 8.3, household bleach about 12.5.
An estimated due date from the first day of the last menstrual period, using Naegele's rule (280 days).
Gestational age today is computed live from the entered LMP to the current date, so it changes day by day; the due date itself does not change once the LMP is fixed.

Estimated due date = first day of last menstrual period + 280 days (40 weeks). This is Naegele’s rule. It assumes a regular 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14, which is why the approximate conception date is shown as LMP + 14 days. Trimester boundaries shown are LMP + 14 weeks and LMP + 28 weeks.
