. Approximate conception (28-day cycle assumption) is 2026-01-15. On the reference date 2026-09-10, gestational age is (2026-09-10 − 2026-01-01) = 252 days =

, with 28 days (4 weeks 0 days) remaining to the estimated due date. Use Reset example above to reproduce the due date; gestational age today on the live page is computed from the actual current date.

Naegele’s rule is an estimate built on two assumptions that often do not hold exactly: a regular 28-day cycle and ovulation on day 14. Longer or irregular cycles, uncertain LMP dates, and ultrasound dating can all shift the estimate, and the actual date of delivery varies from person to person — only a minority of births fall exactly on the estimated date. This page is not a substitute for prenatal care records or clinical dating, and it makes no claim about the health of any pregnancy.
Adding 280 days (40 weeks) to the first day of the last menstrual period. It is the standard back-of-the-envelope dating rule, not a measurement.
Because cycles vary: ovulation is not always on day 14, cycle lengths differ, and the LMP date itself can be uncertain. Ultrasound dating often refines the estimate.
Then ovulation likely came later than day 14, and the true due date may be later than this estimate. The page does not adjust for cycle length — that adjustment belongs in clinical dating.
No. It is an estimate at the centre of a range; actual delivery dates vary widely around it.
No. Use prenatal care records and clinical advice for medical decisions; this page only shows the arithmetic of Naegele's rule.
Today's value of a future sum at a given discount rate — the time value of money, with the discount amount shown alongside.
Annual compounding. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

, where FV is the future sum, r is the annual discount rate as a decimal, and n is the number of years. The discount is FV − PV: the amount the future sum loses by waiting. This is the mirror image of compound growth — the future value formula run backwards.
= 10,000 ÷ 1.6289 = $6,139.13. The discount is 10,000 − 6,139.13 = $3,860.87. At 5 years instead, the same sum is worth 10,000 ÷ 1.05

This page discounts a single lump sum at a constant annual rate with annual compounding. It does not handle a series of payments (that needs an annuity calculation), a changing rate over time, monthly compounding, taxes, or inflation adjustments — a nominal discount rate and a real (inflation-adjusted) rate give different answers. The rate you pick is doing all the work: a small change in r moves the present value a lot over long horizons, so treat the result as a comparison tool, not a market price.

Because money today can be invested and grown. $6,139.13 invested at 5% for 10 years becomes $10,000, so the two amounts are equivalent at that rate — neither is a bargain, they are the same value at different times.

It depends on the question. For an investment decision, use your expected return or cost of capital. For comparing offers, use the same rate for every option so the comparison is fair. There is no single correct rate.
They are inverses. Future value grows a present sum forward (multiply by (1 + r)
Lower. A higher discount rate means future money is penalised more heavily, so its present value falls. At 10% instead of 5%, the same $10,000 in 10 years is worth only $3,855.43.
, which makes the present value slightly smaller than the annual-compounding figure. This page uses annual compounding and says so; for monthly schedules, adjust the rate and periods accordingly.
Bars are scaled to the larger profit. A shorter new-profit bar means the increase loses money despite the higher price.
Price, cost, sales, and the price increase are held at the values above; only the volume decline changes across rows.

New price = price × (1 + increase%). New volume = sales × (1 − volume decline%). New profit = (new price − cost) × new volume. Current profit = (price − cost) × sales. Profit change = new profit − current profit.

Price $199, cost $110, sales 1,000 units, increase 8%, volume decline 5%: new price = $199 × 1.08 = $214.92, new volume = 1,000 × 0.95 = 950 units, new profit = ($214.92 − $110) × 950 = $99,674, current profit = ($199 − $110) × 1,000 = $89,000, so profit rises by $10,674.

Unit cost stays constant and the volume decline is entered by you, not predicted. Fixed costs, competitor responses, customer switching over time, and demand shifts are not modeled — treat the result as a scenario comparison, not a forecast.
Profit change = (price × (1 + increase%) − cost) × sales × (1 − volume decline%) − (price − cost) × sales. The new margin per unit times the new volume, minus today's profit.
Yes. If the volume lost outweighs the extra margin per unit, new profit falls below current profit. That is exactly the trade this calculator exposes.
Volume changes can move unit cost in reality, but this model isolates the price-volume trade. If your unit cost changes with volume, adjust the cost input and compare scenarios.
They cancel out of the change: both scenarios bear the same fixed costs, so the difference in profit is driven by unit margin and volume alone.
No. Combine it with customer research, competitor pricing, and a margin check — the volume decline you enter is the most uncertain input, so test several values.
Saved layouts, language preferences and optional device-only usage history are stored in this browser. Use this button to remove CalcMintly local data.
Net profit, net margin, total cost, and cost ratio from revenue and costs.
Total cost is variable plus fixed costs. Cost ratio is total cost divided by revenue.
Bars are scaled to the larger of total cost and profit. When costs exceed revenue, the profit bar is shown in amber and the verdict flags the loss.
Net profit = revenue − variable costs − fixed costs. Net margin = net profit ÷ revenue × 100%. Total cost = variable costs + fixed costs. Cost ratio = total cost ÷ revenue × 100%.

Revenue $100,000, variable costs $68,000, fixed costs $8,000: total cost = $76,000, net profit = $100,000 − $76,000 = $24,000, net margin = $24,000 ÷ $100,000 × 100% = 24.00%, and cost ratio = 76.00%.

This is an operating view: interest, taxes, depreciation, and one-off items are not separated out. If your cost figures already include them, the margin reflects that; if not, it does not. Costs are treated as fixed totals for the period, not per-unit rates.
Net profit = revenue − variable costs − fixed costs; net margin = net profit ÷ revenue. It splits a period's revenue into what costs consumed and what remained.
Variable costs move with output — materials, per-order fees. Fixed costs do not — rent, base salaries. The split matters for break-even analysis; for net profit only the total matters.
Costs exceeded revenue for the period: a loss of that amount. The margin is negative by the same proportion.
No. Gross margin stops at cost of goods sold; net margin counts all variable and fixed costs entered here, so it is usually lower.
No, unless tax is already inside the cost figures you enter. Apply tax treatment separately to the net profit.
Margin divides by revenue, so at zero revenue it is undefined. Profit itself is still shown as negative total costs.
Solve ax squared plus bx plus c equals zero: both roots, the discriminant, the vertex, and complex roots when the discriminant is negative.
x² − 5x + 6 = 0: a = 1, b = −5, c = 6. Discriminant = (−5)² − 4 × 1 × 6 = 25 − 24 = 1. Roots = [5 ± √1] ÷ 2, so x = 3 and x = 2. Check: 3² − 15 + 6 = 0 and 2² − 10 + 6 = 0. The vertex is at x = 2.5.

Only genuine quadratics are solved: a must not be zero. If a = 0 the equation is linear (bx + c = 0) and this page says so instead of dividing by zero. Coefficients may be decimals or negative. Very large coefficients can lose precision in floating-point arithmetic; results are rounded to two decimals for display, so a root like 0.001 may show as 0.
Then it is not a quadratic at all — it is the linear equation bx + c = 0, with the single solution x = −c ÷ b (when b is not zero either). This page flags that case instead of producing nonsense.
Whether the roots are real and how many: positive means two distinct real roots, zero means one repeated root, negative means no real roots — the parabola never crosses the x-axis.

When the discriminant is negative, the roots involve i (the square root of −1). For x² + 2x + 5 = 0 the roots are −1 + 2i and −1 − 2i. They are genuine solutions over the complex numbers, just not points on the real x-axis.
A degree-2 polynomial has two roots counting multiplicity. They can coincide (one repeated root) or be a complex pair, but there are always two.
Factoring is faster when the roots are small integers, as in the example (x − 3)(x − 2). The formula always works, including when factoring is not obvious.
Compare your current mortgage with a new loan side by side: monthly payment, total interest, break-even month, and whether the refinance pays off before you move.
Total interest for the current loan counts only the remaining term, not interest already paid.
Bars are scaled to the larger of the two totals. A lower payment can still mean more total interest when the new term is longer — check the verdict above.

Cumulative saving counts only months where both loans are being repaid. After either loan ends, the comparison changes. Closing costs are recovered once cumulative saving passes them — that month is the break-even point.
− 1]. Break-even months = closing costs ÷ monthly saving. Total interest = monthly payment × payments − balance.

Balance $300,000, current 7% with 20 years left: payment $2,325.90. New 5% for 20 years: payment $1,979.87, saving $346.03/month. With $4,000 closing costs, break-even is $4,000 ÷ $346.03 = 11.56 months. Total interest falls from $258,215.23 to $175,168.13 — a $83,047.10 saving — and break-even arrives well inside a 10-year stay, so on these numbers the refinance pays off.

Both loans are fixed-rate with no fees beyond the closing-cost input, no cash-out, and no change in balance at refinancing. Taxes, insurance, HOA dues, and private mortgage insurance are not included. A longer new term can lower the payment while raising total interest — the comparison table shows that trade directly. Rate changes, points bought separately from closing costs, and tax effects are not modeled.
No. Extending the term can cut the monthly payment but add years of interest. Compare total interest as well as the monthly figure — the table above does both.
The month when cumulative monthly savings first cover closing costs. If you move or refinance again before break-even, the refinance may not have paid off.

Then the savings never repay the closing costs. Enter your planned stay above and the verdict checks this for you: a refinance that breaks even after your move is flagged, even if the monthly saving looks good.

Yes, unless the new term matches your remaining term. A new 20-year loan on a mortgage with 20 years left keeps the date; a new 30-year loan pushes it out 10 years, which is usually why total interest rises despite a lower payment.
Yes, in closing costs. Points buy a lower rate, so they belong in the break-even calculation, not as a separate saving.
No. It assumes the new rate stays fixed for the whole new term. If the new rate can adjust, the saving and break-even figures are only valid until the first adjustment.

Estimate the monthly value of working remotely: commute spending and recovered time, minus extra home costs.
Cash saving is commute spending saved minus extra home costs. Time value is recovered hours times hourly value. The total combines both.
Bars compare the cash half with the time half. The cash bar is floored at zero for display when cash saving is negative — the table shows the true figure.
Each row reuses your daily commute figures and hourly value and varies only remote days. Home costs are monthly and fixed, so few remote days look worse per day.
Monthly value = remote days × (daily commute spending + commute minutes ÷ 60 × hourly value) − extra home costs. Cash saving = remote days × daily commute spending − extra home costs.

Commute $45 per day, 90 minutes per day, hourly value $80, 12 remote days, extra home costs $300. Per day: $45 + 90 ÷ 60 × $80 = $45 + $120 = $165. Gross = 12 × $165 = $1,980. Total = $1,980 − $300 = $1,680 per month. Cash-only (hourly value zero): 12 × $45 − $300 = $240 per month. Recovered time = 12 × 1.5 = 18 hours.

Set hourly value to zero for a cash-only comparison: recovered time is not automatically spendable income, and valuing it at full hourly cost overstates the benefit if it is absorbed by household tasks or rest. Extra home costs are a single monthly figure — heating, electricity, equipment, and food increases must all be inside it or the cash saving is overstated. Commute spending should be after any employer subsidy, and the model does not cover career, collaboration, or wellbeing effects in either direction.
Each remote day is worth daily commute spending plus commute minutes divided by 60 times hourly value; multiply by remote days and subtract extra monthly home costs.
Only if the recovered time earns or saves money. For a cash-only view, set hourly value to zero — the worked example's cash-only figure is $240, not $1,680.
The increase in heating, electricity, internet, equipment, and food caused by working from home, for the month. If you would pay most of it anyway, do not count it.
Because home costs are monthly and fixed while savings scale with days. One remote day a month rarely covers a full month of extra home costs on cash alone.
Yes: minutes and spending should be the full round trip for the day, not one leg. Halving either input halves the daily value.
No. Less commuting may improve wellbeing and focus, while less office presence may affect visibility and collaboration. Those are real but outside this money-and-time model.

Model how much profit returns erode through lost profit, reverse shipping, and product loss.

Erosion counts three parts per return: the profit that order would have kept, the reverse-shipping cost, and the share of product value lost. Avoid double-counting costs already inside the profit figure.
The erosion bar is drawn against profit with no returns, so the share of profit lost is visible.
Orders and per-return costs are held at the values above; only the return rate changes across rows.
Profit erosion = orders × return rate% × (profit per order + reverse shipping + returned value × loss%). Returned orders = orders × return rate%.

Orders 3,000, return rate 12%, profit per order $45, reverse shipping $18, returned value $120, loss 25%: returned orders = 3,000 × 0.12 = 360, erosion per return = $45 + $18 + $120 × 0.25 = $93, and total erosion = 360 × $93 = $33,480.

Includes foregone profit, reverse shipping, and product loss under your assumptions. Restocking fees recovered, resold returned stock, and fixed warehousing costs are not modeled. If your profit-per-order figure already nets off shipping or expected returns, adjust it first to avoid double-counting.

Profit erosion = orders × return rate% × (profit per order + reverse shipping + returned value × loss%). Each return costs the profit it would have kept, plus shipping it back, plus the share of product value written off.
The share of a returned product's value that cannot be recovered — damage, missing parts, or unsellable condition. A 25% loss on a $120 item is $30 per return.
Eroded profit divided by the profit all orders would have earned with no returns. At the example values it is $33,480 ÷ $135,000 = 24.80%.
Only if your profit-per-order figure already deducts reverse shipping. If it does, set reverse shipping to $0 or adjust the profit figure — the FAQ and scope note flag this.
Not modeled: a resold return recovers most of the product value, so the loss percentage for those units should be near zero. Use a blended loss rate across all returns.
The three levers are the return rate, reverse-shipping cost, and product loss rate. The scenario table shows how much each point of return rate costs at your volumes.
Missing sides and angles of a right triangle from its two legs — hypotenuse, angles, area, and perimeter.
The two sides meeting at the right angle. All lengths in the same unit. Results update as you type. All calculations run locally in your browser.

Pythagoras: hypotenuse c = √(a² + b²). The acute angles come from the sides: the angle opposite leg a is arctan(a ÷ b), and the angle opposite leg b is 90° minus that angle — the two acute angles always add to 90°. Area = ½ × a × b, and perimeter = a + b + c.

Legs 3 and 4: hypotenuse = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. The angle opposite the side of 3 is arctan(3 ÷ 4) = 36.87°, so the other acute angle is 90 − 36.87 = 53.13°. Area = ½ × 3 × 4 = 6, and perimeter = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. The 3–4–5 triangle is the smallest right triangle with whole-number sides, which is why it shows up everywhere from building sites to textbook problems.

This page takes the two legs of a right triangle. It does not solve triangles given a hypotenuse and one leg, or given an angle and a side — for those, use Pythagoras or trigonometry directly on the same formulas above. It assumes the angle between the two entered sides is exactly 90°; for any other triangle, these formulas do not apply. Angles display in degrees to two decimals.

It is Pythagoras' theorem: in a right triangle, the square built on the hypotenuse has the same area as the two squares built on the legs combined. It holds for every right triangle, not just whole-number ones.

The smallest right triangle with whole-number sides: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5². Builders have used knotted ropes in 3–4–5 proportions for millennia to lay out exact right angles, since any multiple (6–8–10, 9–12–15) works the same way.

From the ratio of the legs: the angle opposite leg a satisfies tan(angle) = a ÷ b, so angle = arctan(a ÷ b). The second acute angle is 90° minus the first, because a triangle's angles sum to 180° and the right angle already takes 90°.
Not on this page — it expects the two legs. If you know the hypotenuse c and one leg a, the other leg is √(c² − a²), which you can compute and then enter here.
Only that both legs use the same unit: the hypotenuse, area, and perimeter then come out in that unit and its square. Mixing metres and centimetres gives a wrong answer, so convert first.
Pythagoras does not apply. General triangles need the law of cosines (c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C) or the triangle area calculator's Heron formula, depending on what you know.

No, unless the values you enter already reflect them. Brokerage fees, taxes on gains, and inflation all reduce the real return.
Not necessarily. ROI says nothing about risk, volatility, or how long the money was tied up. A high ROI on a risky, illiquid investment is not directly comparable to a lower ROI on a safe one.

Monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12. Grown current amount = current amount × (1 + monthly rate)

− 1) ÷ monthly rate]. If the grown current amount already reaches the target, the required contribution is $0.

The rate is assumed constant, contributions are never missed, and taxes, fees, and inflation are ignored, so the target is in nominal dollars. If the current amount already grows past the target, no contribution is required and the plan is already funded on these assumptions.

Because interest covers more of the gap. But a higher assumed rate is also a riskier assumption: if the real return is lower, the plan falls short.

Estimate how many months it takes a side hustle to recover its startup cost from monthly contribution.
Monthly contribution is profit per order times monthly orders minus monthly fixed costs. Break-even divides the startup cost by that contribution.
Bars compare the startup cost with a full year of contribution. If the year bar clears the startup bar, break-even falls inside 12 months.
Each row is cumulative contribution minus the startup cost, assuming the same orders, profit, and fixed costs throughout. Early months are negative until the startup cost is recovered.

Months to break even = startup cost ÷ (profit per order × monthly orders − monthly fixed costs). Orders to recover the cost = startup cost ÷ profit per order. Net after N months = monthly contribution × N − startup cost.

Startup $20,000, fixed costs $1,200 per month, profit $85 per order, 60 orders per month. Monthly contribution = $85 × 60 − $1,200 = $5,100 − $1,200 = $3,900. Months to break even = $20,000 ÷ $3,900 = 5.13 months. Orders to recover the cost = $20,000 ÷ $85 = 235.29 orders. Net after 12 months = $3,900 × 12 − $20,000 = $26,800.

Monthly contribution must be positive for any break-even to exist; if fixed costs exceed gross contribution, the model reports no break-even rather than a negative time. Sales and margins are assumptions, not guaranteed demand, and the model assumes they stay constant — seasonality, churn, price changes, and growth are not modeled. Financing costs, tax, payment timing, refunds, and the value of the founder's time are excluded unless folded into fixed costs or profit per order.
Monthly contribution is profit per order times monthly orders minus monthly fixed costs; months to break even are the startup cost divided by that contribution.

Then there is no break-even: the hustle loses money or stands still every month, and the startup cost is never recovered. Fix contribution first — more orders, higher profit per order, or lower fixed costs.
It means the startup cost has been repaid. From that month onward, monthly contribution is profit before tax and before the founder's time, if neither is counted in the inputs.
If you want an honest answer, yes — value the hours at a reasonable rate and include them, or the break-even flatters a hustle that only works by donating unpaid labour.
235.29 orders is the arithmetic answer; in practice it means the 236th order is the one that tips the cumulative total past the startup cost, part-way through the break-even month.
Financing, tax, refunds, seasonality, and demand risk. Treat the month count as a planning figure at assumed sales, and re-run it at half sales to see the downside case.

The engagement multiplier is engagement divided by 4, clamped between 0.7 and 1.5, so very low or very high engagement cannot move the rate without limit.

Sponsor rate = views ÷ 1,000 × CPM × clamp(engagement ÷ 4, 0.7, 1.5) + production hours × hourly cost. The 85%–120% range shown is the estimate times 0.85 and 1.20.

Views 80,000, CPM $120, engagement 4.5%, production 16 hours at $200. Multiplier = 4.5 ÷ 4 = 1.125, inside the 0.7–1.5 clamp. CPM-based value = 80,000 ÷ 1,000 × $120 × 1.125 = $10,800. Past performance, audience fit, and deliverables still decide what a sponsor will actually pay.

Because two creators with the same view count do not deliver the same attention. The 4% reference point means engagement above 4% lifts the rate and below 4% reduces it, within the clamp.

Area = length × width. Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). Purchase area = area × (1 + waste rate).

Length 6 m, width 4 m: area = 6 × 4 = 24 m², perimeter = 2 × (6 + 4) = 20 m. At an 8% waste allowance, waste area = 24 × 0.08 = 1.92 m², so purchase area = 25.92 m² (279 ft²). These are the example defaults above; replace them with your own measurements.

Mean, population standard deviation and sample standard deviation for a list of numbers.
Sample SD is undefined for a single value (it divides by n − 1 = 0) and is shown as — in that case.
Mean = Σx ÷ n. Population SD = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n]; sample SD uses n − 1 in place of n. Population variance is Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n and sample variance is Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1).

For 12, 15, 18, 20, 25: mean = 90 ÷ 5 = 18. Squared deviations are 36, 9, 0, 4 and 49, summing to 98. Population SD = √(98 ÷ 5) = √19.6 = 4.4272 (4.427189 to more places). Sample SD = √(98 ÷ 4) = √24.5 = 4.9497. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result, then replace the list with your own data.
Population SD (÷ n) when your numbers are the whole group you care about. Sample SD (÷ n − 1) when they are a sample and you are estimating the spread of a larger population.
It divides by n − 1 instead of n, which corrects for the fact that a sample mean is fitted to the sample itself. The gap shrinks as n grows.
Population SD is 0 (no spread), and sample SD is undefined, shown as —, because n − 1 is zero.

Solve two linear equations for x and y by the determinant method, with a check of both equations.

2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2: D = 2 × (−1) − 1 × 1 = −3. Then x = (7 × (−1) − 2 × 1) ÷ (−3) = (−9) ÷ (−3) = 3, and y = (2 × 2 − 1 × 7) ÷ (−3) = (−3) ÷ (−3) = 1. Check: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, and 3 − 1 = 2. Both equations hold, so (3, 1) is the single crossing point of the two lines.
After Gabriel Cramer, who published the determinant method in 1750. It is the same elimination you would do by hand — multiply, subtract, solve — compressed into two formulas.

Yes, and you should get the same answer. From x − y = 2, x = y + 2; substituting into 2x + y = 7 gives 2(y + 2) + y = 7, so 3y = 3, y = 1, x = 3. Substitution is easier by hand for simple systems; determinants scale better.
Yes for this method. If either equation contains x², y², xy, or a square root of x or y, the determinant formulas do not apply, and the system can have zero, one, two, or more solutions.
Substitute x and y back into both original equations, as the page's check chips do. A correct solution makes both sides equal in both equations; a solution that satisfies only one equation is wrong.

Your selected level is the headline result; the other rows show how much the category choice alone moves the estimate.
Bars are scaled to the extremely-active value for your BMR. All values are kcal/day.

TDEE = Mifflin–St Jeor BMR × activity factor, where BMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age + 5 for men or − 161 for women. Activity factors used here: 1.2 sedentary, 1.375 lightly active, 1.55 moderately active, 1.725 very active, 1.9 extremely active.
Weight 65 kg, height 170 cm, age 30, female, lightly active (1.375): BMR = 10 × 65 + 6.25 × 170 − 5 × 30 − 161 =

, or 13,490 kcal per week, of which 525.6 kcal/day is the activity increment above BMR. At the sedentary factor the same BMR gives 1,681.8 kcal/day; at extremely active it gives 2,662.9 kcal/day. Use Reset example above to reproduce this result.

TDEE inherits the limits of both parts: BMR is a population equation that varies between individuals, and the activity factor is a coarse category chosen by judgment, not a measurement of actual days. Two people picking the same label can have quite different true activity, and day-to-day variation is averaged away. The result is a planning estimate, not a measured daily burn.
BMR is resting expenditure only. TDEE multiplies BMR by an activity factor to include everything else a day involves.

Judge a typical week honestly: mostly sitting is sedentary, light daily movement is lightly active, regular training is moderately active, hard daily training is very active. When in doubt, the lower category is the more cautious estimate.
Because the factor multiplies the whole BMR: moving from 1.2 to 1.9 raises the example result by about 58%, so a wrong category is the largest error source on this page.
No. It is an estimate of expenditure, not a recommendation for intake. Intake decisions involve goals and circumstances this page does not model.
Yes — weight, age, and activity all feed the equation, so re-entering current values gives a current estimate.

Convert a time of day between UTC offsets, with the day shift shown explicitly.
Offsets are fixed numbers of hours from UTC. They do not encode daylight-saving rules, which change by place and date.

Target time = source time − source UTC offset + target UTC offset, wrapped to 24 hours. In minutes: target minutes = hour × 60 + minute − source offset × 60 + target offset × 60; if the result is negative, add 1,440 (24 hours) and count one day earlier; if it reaches 1,440 or more, subtract 1,440 and count one day later.

Offsets in the dropdowns are standard-time examples for the named places. Several places shift by one hour during daylight saving, and governments occasionally change offset rules — the offset that applies on a specific date must be confirmed with an official source for that place and date.

09:00 at UTC+8 is 9 × 60 = 540 minutes; 540 − 480 (UTC+8) + (−300) (UTC−5) = −240 minutes. Adding 1,440 gives 1,200 minutes = 20:00, one day earlier — so 09:00 in Beijing is 20:00 the previous day in New York standard time.

This page converts times of day using fixed UTC offsets only. It does not know dates, daylight-saving transitions, or historical offset changes, and it cannot tell you whether a given place observes daylight saving on a given date. For scheduling, confirm the offset for the actual date with an official source. Times are given to the minute; seconds are not handled.

No. The offsets are fixed numbers. A place on daylight saving is typically one hour ahead of its standard offset — for example New York is UTC−4 on daylight saving instead of UTC−5. Check the offset for your actual date.
Because subtracting the offsets can push the time before midnight. 09:00 in Beijing is still the previous evening in New York — the day shift makes that explicit instead of silently showing 20:00.
They are included: UTC+05:30 (India) and UTC+09:30 (Adelaide, standard) are in the dropdowns, and the formula works in minutes so they convert exactly.
Not on this page: it converts a time of day plus a day shift. For a dated event, apply the day shift to your date by hand and confirm daylight saving for that date.
London is UTC+00:00 in winter and UTC+01:00 (British Summer Time) in summer. The dropdown gives the standard offset; pick +01:00 for summer dates.
